docs.title: Porthole
docs.text:
A self-hosted phone remote for Claude Code and Codex sessions running on your own machine. No cloud in the path of your sessions, no accounts: a small daemon on the computer, an app on the phone, and your VPN in between.

  • Attach to sessions you already started in tmux, or start new ones in any repository.
  • Read the conversation as rendered markdown, straight from the CLIs' own transcript files. Tool calls, results and thinking are all there.
  • Type prompts and slash commands (/compact, your own skills) into the real TUI, and drop into a terminal view for permission prompts and menus.
  • Approve Claude Code permission prompts from the phone.
  • See which account is doing the work and how much quota is left (with claude-swap installed).

The daemon only listens on loopback, private and VPN addresses and refuses to start on a public one. Phones pair by scanning a one-time QR code, pin the daemon's certificate, and can be revoked at any time.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text: Piece Where it runs What it does Daemon (porthole) the computer that runs Claude Code or Codex (Linux or macOS) watches transcript files, drives tmux, brokers permission prompts, serves the app over TLS on port 7433 App Android or iOS lists sessions, renders conversations, sends input, answers permission prompts VPN between the two any private network the phone can reach the computer on: the same Wi-Fi, WireGuard, Tailscale, NetBird Push relay (optional) a Cloudflare Worker, hosted by the project or by you wakes the phone while the app is closed; sees only ciphertext

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
On the computer:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZerkerEOD/porthole/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
cd ~/code/my-project && porthole add     # optional: offer this repository in the app
porthole pair                            # shows a QR code

On the phone: install the app, tap Scan pairing code, point it at the QR. That is the whole setup. Follow the detailed path if anything needs explaining:

  1. Install the daemon
  2. Pair a phone
  3. The app

docs.title: Get the app
docs.text:
• iOS: a public TestFlight link, https://testflight.apple.com/join/wYZrvvYa, is used for the beta. It starts working once Apple's beta review has passed; if it reports that the beta is not accepting testers yet, check back shortly.
  • Android: the Play closed test link will be added here once the test track is live.
  • Build it yourself: the Flutter project is in app/; see The app.

Source code and daemon releases: https://github.com/ZerkerEOD/porthole.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Sessions: what the app can see and control, and why tmux matters.
  • Push notifications: alerts while the app is closed.
  • Configuration and the CLI reference.
  • Self-host the push relay.
  • Troubleshooting and the security model.

docs.title: Porthole privacy policy
docs.text: The privacy policy for Porthole (app, daemon and relay) lives at https://zerkersec.io/privacy, together with the policy for the site and the supporter programme. It is maintained in one place so the app, the stores and this repository never drift apart. Section 6 covers the app and daemon, section 7 the relay.

docs.title: Porthole terms of service
docs.text: The terms for Porthole store builds, the relay and the supporter programme live at https://zerkersec.io/terms. The software itself is licensed under the AGPL-3.0 with the additional permission in LICENSE-EXCEPTION.md; the terms do not narrow that licence.

docs.title: The app
docs.text: The Porthole app runs on Android and iOS. It sells nothing, has no accounts, and talks only to the daemons you paired with (and, if you turn it on, a push relay).

docs.title: Install it
docs.text:
• iOS: join the beta through the public TestFlight link, https://testflight.apple.com/join/wYZrvvYa. The link becomes active after Apple's beta review; if TestFlight says the beta is not accepting testers yet, try again later.
  • Android: the Play closed test link will be added here once the test track is live.

docs.title: Build it yourself
docs.text:
app/ is a Flutter project (Android, iOS, and Linux desktop for development):

cd app
flutter build apk      # Android
flutter build ios      # iOS

A build made this way has everything except push: without the Firebase options compiled in there is no Push relay field in Settings at all. Notifications still work while the app is open, and on Android with the background service. To build with push you need your own Firebase project and --dart-define-from-file=dart_defines/store.json; see Self-hosting the push relay.

docs.title: First launch
docs.text:
The empty home screen offers two things:

  • Scan pairing code starts pairing.
  • Try the demo loads a sample machine with canned sessions so you can look around before pairing anything.

docs.title: Home
docs.text: Every session from every connected machine, filtered by All, a machine, Claude or Codex. Sessions that need you (a permission prompt, a question) float to the top with a badge. Finished sessions are under History. The New session button starts an agent on a repository of a connected machine. A machine's menu offers Connect now, Accounts & usage, Open machine view and Manage machines.

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
The conversation rendered from the CLI's own transcript: prompts, replies, tool calls and results, and (with Show thinking) the model's thinking. Scroll up to Load earlier. The input bar types into the real TUI, so slash commands and your own skills work exactly as they do at the keyboard.

  • Terminal view switches to the live tmux pane for menus, prompts and anything the chat view cannot show, with a key bar for Enter, Escape, arrows and control keys.
  • Interrupt (Esc) stops the agent mid-turn.
  • Resume in tmux… restarts a finished session inside tmux so it becomes controllable.
  • A permission request appears as a card with the tool name and input and Allow / Deny buttons.

The header shows the machine, session status, repository, model and the account doing the work. A session that is not running inside tmux shows a read-only notice; see Sessions.

docs.title: New session
docs.text: Pick the machine, Claude Code or Codex, a repository (see choosing where sessions start), a permission mode for Claude Code (Default (ask), Plan mode, Accept edits) and an optional first prompt. The session runs inside a tmux session you can also attach to from a terminal.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text: One entry per paired daemon with its reported name, version and running sessions. Rename it, toggle Auto-connect (connect when the app opens), Mute notifications (no alerts or push from this machine), Connect now, or Forget it. Pair machine adds another.

docs.title: Accounts & usage
docs.text: With claude-swap installed on the machine, this screen shows which account is active and how much of each quota window is used. Codex rate limits are shown when the CLI reports them.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
• Notify while connected: local notifications for permission prompts and input requests while the app is open (or kept alive).
  • Stay connected in the background (Android): a foreground service keeps the VPN socket open with a persistent notification, so alerts arrive without any cloud service.
  • Push relay: notifications while the app is closed. See Push notifications.
  • Machines: the same list as above.
  • Links to the privacy policy, terms of service and source code.

docs.title: Install the daemon
docs.text:
The daemon runs on the computer where Claude Code or Codex runs, as your own user. It needs:

  • Linux or macOS.
  • tmux, for sessions you want to control from the phone.
  • claude and/or codex on your PATH.
  • A private address the phone can reach: the same Wi-Fi, or a VPN such as WireGuard, Tailscale or NetBird. The daemon never listens on a public address.

docs.title: One-line installer
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZerkerEOD/porthole/main/scripts/install.sh | sh

The script downloads the latest GitHub release for your OS and architecture, verifies the checksum, and runs porthole install.

Prefer to build from source? You need Go 1.27:

cd daemon
go build -o ~/.local/bin/porthole ./cmd/porthole
porthole install

docs.title: What porthole install does
docs.text:
1. Copies the running binary to ~/.local/bin/porthole if it is not already there.
  2. Sets up a user service so the daemon starts at login and restarts if it crashes:
    • Linux: writes ~/.config/systemd/user/porthole.service, runs systemctl --user daemon-reload and systemctl --user enable --now porthole, then tries loginctl enable-linger so the service also runs while you are logged out. If linger needs root it prints the sudo command to run.
    • macOS: writes ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.zerkersec.porthole.daemon.plist and loads it.
  3. Runs the same checks as porthole doctor: tmux, the CLIs, the profiles it will watch, and whether the daemon answers.
  4. Installs the Claude Code hooks and the Codex notify handler, exactly like porthole install-hooks. Hooks are what turn permission prompts into something the phone can answer; they apply to sessions started after this point.
  5. Prints the next steps: porthole add inside a repository, then porthole pair.

porthole install --no-service skips step 2 (run porthole serve yourself, or use the unit files under daemon/packaging/). --no-hooks skips step 4.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
porthole status

prints the version, the addresses the daemon is listening on, and how many sessions and devices it knows about. porthole doctor goes through the environment in more detail.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text: The app connects to TCP port 7433 (change it with port in config.toml). If the computer runs a host firewall, allow that port on the VPN or LAN interface the phone will use.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Tell the daemon about your repositories with porthole add (optional: everything you have already used an agent in is listed automatically).
  • Pair a phone.

docs.title: Pair a phone
docs.text: Pairing gives the phone a device token and the daemon's certificate fingerprint. It happens once per phone and machine; after that the app reconnects on its own.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The daemon must be running (porthole status answers).
  • The phone must be able to reach the computer on a private address: the same Wi-Fi network, or a VPN such as WireGuard, Tailscale or NetBird. The daemon refuses connections from public addresses, so there is no way to pair across the open internet.
  • TCP port 7433 must be open in the computer's firewall on that interface.

docs.title: Scan the code
docs.text:
On the computer:

porthole pair

prints a QR code, how long it is valid, and the same values as text:

Scan with the Porthole app within 2m0s.
Manual entry: host 100.64.0.5 or 192.168.1.20  port 7433  code ABCDEFGH
Certificate fingerprint: …

In the app, tap Scan pairing code (the empty home screen) or Machines → Pair machine, and point the camera at the QR. The code is single use and expires after two minutes; run porthole pair again if you miss the window.

If the output ends with warning: no VPN or private address is bound; is your VPN up?, the daemon found nothing but loopback to listen on. Bring the VPN up and restart the daemon.

docs.title: Enter the values by hand
docs.text:
Tap Enter manually on the pairing screen if the camera is not an option. The fields are:

Field From porthole pair Host (VPN address) one of the host values; pick the one on the network the phone is on Port port (7433 unless you changed it) Certificate fingerprint the Certificate fingerprint line Pairing code code This device's name anything you like; it is what porthole devices lists

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• porthole pair --label "Aaron's phone" attaches a label to the pairing.
  • porthole pair --json prints the pairing payload as JSON instead of a QR, for scripting or for feeding a second screen.

docs.title: What pairing establishes
docs.text:
• The app pins the daemon's self-signed TLS certificate by fingerprint and refuses anything else, so there is no certificate authority to manage.
  • The app receives a random device token, stored in the phone's keychain or keystore; the daemon stores only a hash of it.
  • The two sides agree on a key used to encrypt push notices, so a relay (if you use one) never sees their contents.

See Security for the full model.

docs.title: Manage paired devices
docs.text:
porthole devices              # ID, name, paired date, last seen
porthole devices revoke <id>  # closes that phone's connections within a second

On the phone, Machines lists every daemon you have paired: rename it, mute its notifications, turn auto-connect on or off, or forget it. One phone can pair with as many machines as you like, and they share a single session list.

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
porthole is one binary: the daemon (porthole serve) and the commands that talk to it over a local socket. Run them as the user who owns the sessions, never as root.

Global flags, accepted by every command:

Flag Meaning --config <file> configuration file (default ~/.config/porthole/config.toml) --log-level <level> debug, info, warn or error (default info) --version print the version

docs.title: install
docs.text:
porthole install [--no-service] [--no-hooks]

Puts the running binary in ~/.local/bin/porthole if it is not already there, sets up a user service that starts the daemon at login, runs the doctor checks and installs the hooks, then prints what to do next.

  • Linux: writes ~/.config/systemd/user/porthole.service, runs systemctl --user daemon-reload and systemctl --user enable --now porthole, and tries loginctl enable-linger so the daemon runs while you are logged out (prints the sudo command if that fails).
  • macOS: writes ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.zerkersec.porthole.daemon.plist and loads it.
Flag Meaning --no-service do not create or start a service --no-hooks skip install-hooks

docs.title: doctor
docs.text:
porthole doctor

Prints the config file in use, the workspaces, where tmux, claude, codex and cswap were found, each Claude Code and Codex profile the daemon will watch and whether the hooks are installed in it, and whether the daemon is running and on which addresses.

docs.title: install-hooks
docs.text:
porthole install-hooks [--profile <dir>] [--codex-home <dir>] [--no-claude] [--no-codex]

Adds the Porthole hooks to Claude Code's settings.json and sets Codex's notify handler. Idempotent. Hooks take effect for new sessions; running sessions keep their old hook set.

Flag Meaning --profile <dir> CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR to install into (default ~/.claude) --codex-home <dir> CODEX_HOME to install into (default ~/.codex) --no-claude skip Claude Code --no-codex skip Codex

docs.title: uninstall-hooks
docs.text:
porthole uninstall-hooks [--profile <dir>]

Removes the hooks from Claude Code's settings. Codex's notify = [...] line is removed by hand.

docs.title: config
docs.text:
porthole config

Prints the configuration directory, state directory, socket path and the effective configuration as JSON.

docs.title: serve
docs.text:
porthole serve [--allow-public-bind-i-understand]

Runs the daemon in the foreground. This is what the service runs. It refuses to start as root and refuses to bind a public address.

Flag Meaning --allow-public-bind-i-understand bind and accept connections on public addresses. Not recommended; use a VPN.

docs.title: status
docs.text:
porthole status

Version, machine name, pid, uptime, bound addresses, session and device counts, and whether tmux and cswap were detected.

docs.title: sessions
docs.text:
porthole sessions [--json]

Lists the sessions the daemon knows about: provider, status, the tmux session when controllable, repository, title, last update and id. --json prints the raw records.

docs.title: pair
docs.text:
porthole pair [--label <text>] [--json]

Asks the running daemon for a one-time pairing code and prints it as a QR (porthole://pair?d=…) plus the manual values: hosts, port, code and certificate fingerprint. The code is single use and expires after two minutes. See Pair a phone.

Flag Meaning --label <text> optional label for this pairing --json print the pairing payload as JSON instead of a QR

docs.title: devices
docs.text:
porthole devices
porthole devices revoke <id>

Lists paired phones (id, name, paired date, last seen). revoke deletes one and closes its connections within a second.

docs.title: add
docs.text:
porthole add [dir] [--workspace] [--yes|-y]

Records a repository so the app can start sessions in it. With no argument it uses the current directory. It finds the git top level, shows it, asks to confirm, and writes it to ~/.config/porthole/repos.toml. A running daemon is told to reload at once; otherwise the change applies at the next start.

Flag Meaning --workspace record the directory as a workspace (a parent folder scanned two levels deep for git repositories) instead of a single repository --yes, -y do not ask for confirmation

You only need this for repositories you have not run an agent in yet; everything the daemon has seen a session in is offered automatically.

docs.title: remove
docs.text:
porthole remove [dir]

Removes a repository or workspace recorded by add (current directory when omitted). Entries written by hand in config.toml are edited there.

docs.title: repos
docs.text:
porthole repos

Lists what the app will offer: configured repositories, repositories found under workspaces, and recent directories.

docs.title: wrap
docs.text:
porthole wrap <claude|codex> [args...]

Starts the CLI inside a tmux session in the current directory, so the app can control it, and attaches your terminal. Extra arguments are passed to the CLI. Inside tmux already, it opens a new window instead of nesting.

docs.title: Internal commands
docs.text: porthole hook and porthole codex-notify are what the hooks call; they are hidden and never fail loudly, so the CLIs keep working when the daemon is down. porthole client is a hidden developer tool: a pinned-TLS WebSocket client for exercising the protocol from the command line.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The daemon reads ~/.config/porthole/config.toml (or the file given with --config). The file is optional: with no file at all the daemon listens on every private address on port 7433, watches the default Claude Code and Codex profiles, and offers the repositories it has seen sessions in. porthole config prints the effective values and the paths in use.

Two files live next to each other:

File Who writes it Holds config.toml you everything below; never rewritten by the CLI repos.toml porthole add and porthole remove repos and workspaces lists, merged with the ones in config.toml

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
The full example ships as daemon/packaging/config.example.toml:

# ~/.config/porthole/config.toml
name = "desktop"            # shown in the app
listen = ["auto"]           # every loopback/private/VPN address; or explicit IPs
port = 7433
workspaces = ["~/Programming"]   # parent dirs scanned two levels deep for git repos
repos = []                  # single repos to offer; `porthole add` writes them to repos.toml instead
                            # (directories you have already run claude/codex in appear automatically)
profiles = []               # extra CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR / CODEX_HOME dirs to watch

[claude]
enabled = true
binary = "claude"

[codex]
enabled = true
binary = "codex"

[tmux]
binary = "tmux"
session_prefix = "ph"       # spawned sessions are named ph-<provider>-<id>

[hooks]
permission_timeout_s = 60   # how long a permission prompt waits for the phone

[cswap]
enabled = true              # auto-off when cswap is not on PATH
poll_interval_s = 150       # cache reads; cswap owns the real network cadence

[push]
relay_url = ""              # empty = push off. The relay the app uses, without its credential
                            # (e.g. https://relay.zerkersec.io or your own Worker).

docs.title: Top level
docs.text: name The machine name the app shows. Default: the hostname. listen ["auto"] binds every loopback, RFC1918, CGNAT (100.64.0.0/10), IPv6 ULA and VPN-interface address (tailscale*, wg*, utun*, tun*, nebula*, zt*) on the machine. Give explicit IP addresses instead to bind only those. A public address is refused unless serve is run with --allow-public-bind-i-understand, which is not the intended deployment: use a VPN. Default: ["auto"]. port TCP port for the app. Default: 7433. Open it in the host firewall on the interface the phone uses. workspaces Parent directories scanned two levels deep for git repositories, offered in New session. ~ and environment variables are expanded. porthole add --workspace records the same thing in repos.toml instead. Default: none. repos Individual repositories offered in New session without scanning. porthole add records them in repos.toml; this key is for listing them by hand. Default: none. profiles Extra CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR or CODEX_HOME directories to watch for transcripts, on top of ~/.claude and ~/.codex and anything a running process is using. Default: none.

docs.title: [claude] and [codex]
docs.text: enabled Turn the integration off entirely. Default: true. binary Name or path of the CLI used to start new sessions. Default: claude / codex.

docs.title: [tmux]
docs.text: binary Name or path of tmux. Default: tmux. session_prefix Sessions started from the app are named <prefix>-<provider>-<id>. Default: ph.

docs.title: [hooks]
docs.text: permission_timeout_s How long a Claude Code permission prompt waits for an answer from a phone before falling back to the terminal prompt. Default: 60.

docs.title: [cswap]
docs.text: enabled Read account and quota information from claude-swap. Automatically off when cswap is not on PATH. Default: true. binary Name or path of the cswap binary. Default: cswap. poll_interval_s How often the daemon re-reads cswap's cached account list. cswap decides when to hit the network; this only controls how fresh the app's view is. Default: 150.

docs.title: [push]
docs.text: relay_url Base URL of the push relay, without the credential that sits in the app's relay URL: https://relay.zerkersec.io for the hosted relay, or your own Worker's URL. Empty means push is off and the daemon refuses push registrations from the app. Default: empty. See Push notifications.

docs.title: Reloading
docs.text:
The daemon reloads repos.toml and the workspaces list when porthole add or porthole remove asks it to, or on SIGHUP:

systemctl --user kill -s HUP porthole      # Linux
kill -HUP "$(pgrep -u "$USER" -f 'porthole serve')"

Every other key (port, listen, profiles, the provider, hook, cswap and push sections) needs a restart:

systemctl --user restart porthole                                              # Linux
launchctl kickstart -k "gui/$(id -u)/io.zerkersec.porthole.daemon"            # macOS

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
What Where Override Configuration ~/.config/porthole/ (config.toml, repos.toml) XDG_CONFIG_HOME, --config State: TLS key and certificate, paired devices (devices.json), transcript cursors ~/.local/state/porthole/ (mode 0700) XDG_STATE_HOME Control socket for the CLI and hooks $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/porthole/porthole.sock, or <state>/run/ where there is no runtime dir (macOS) XDG_RUNTIME_DIR Service unit ~/.config/systemd/user/porthole.service (Linux), ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.zerkersec.porthole.daemon.plist (macOS)

Deleting the state directory makes the daemon generate a new certificate and forget every paired phone; you will have to pair again.

docs.title: Push notifications
docs.text:
While the app is open, or kept alive on Android, it hears about permission prompts and finished turns directly from the daemon over the VPN. Once the app is closed (and on iOS, as soon as it leaves the foreground; see iOS background behavior) nothing can reach it except the platform push service. That needs a server holding the app's push credentials, which is the one piece of Porthole that is not on your machine: the push relay.

The relay is optional. Everything else in Porthole works without it.

docs.title: What the relay sees
docs.text: The daemon encrypts a tiny notice (session title, machine name, what kind of attention is needed) with a key agreed at pairing and posts the ciphertext to the relay. The relay checks a signed grant and forwards the ciphertext through FCM to the phone, which decrypts it and shows the notification. The relay sees a push token, a random device id and a timestamp; never a prompt, a repository name or any session content. The app fetches the details from your machine when you open it.

docs.title: Use the hosted relay
docs.text:
The project runs a relay at relay.zerkersec.io for its supporters. Supporting ZerkerEOD at https://zerkersec.io/supporter gives you a personal relay URL of the form

https://PH-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX@relay.zerkersec.io

The part before the @ is your relay credential. The app sends it to the relay as a bearer token and never interprets it.

  1. On the phone: Settings → Push relay, paste the URL, tap Connect. The app asks for notification permission, fetches a grant from the relay, and hands that grant to every paired machine.

  2. On each machine: set the relay's base URL (no credential) in ~/.config/porthole/config.toml and restart the daemon:

    [push]
relay_url = "https://relay.zerkersec.io"

    systemctl --user restart porthole      # Linux

    A daemon with an empty relay_url refuses push registrations, so the app shows the relay as connected but that machine never pushes.

docs.title: Run your own
docs.text: Any relay that speaks the same small API works; the app accepts https://[credential@]host[/path]. See Self-hosting the push relay.

docs.title: Relay status in Settings
docs.text:
Shown as Meaning Relay: connected A grant is held and renews itself. Push is on. Relay: not active The relay refused the credential (HTTP 402: not active, lapsed, or unknown). Check it with whoever runs the relay. Relay: could not verify The relay could not be reached. The app keeps the last grant if it has one and retries.

Grants last at most 30 days and the app renews one within three days of its expiry. If the relay answers 401, 403 or 410 (invalid grant, blocked device, push token gone), the app drops the stored grant and requests a fresh one. Re-check forces a renewal now; Remove relay forgets the URL and tells every machine to stop pushing.

docs.title: Per-machine control
docs.text: Machines → Mute notifications drops that machine's grant, so it neither pushes nor raises live alerts; unmuting restores it. The Push notifications switch in Settings turns push off for every machine without forgetting the relay.

docs.title: Builds without push
docs.text: Push is only possible when the Firebase options are compiled into the app. Store builds have them. A build you made yourself without --dart-define-from-file=dart_defines/store.json has no Push relay field in Settings at all, and shows a note saying so. Notifications still work while the app is open, and on Android with Stay connected in the background.

docs.title: Android without a relay
docs.text: Android can keep the daemon connection alive with a foreground service. Settings → Stay connected in the background turns it on; it shows a persistent notification while a session is open, and alerts arrive straight from the daemon over the VPN with no cloud service involved.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text: A session is one Claude Code or Codex conversation. The daemon finds them by reading the transcript files the CLIs write (~/.claude/projects and ~/.codex/sessions, plus any profiles you configure), so every session shows up in the app whether or not Porthole started it.

docs.title: Controllable or read-only
docs.text:
The app can read any session the daemon can see. It can type into a session only when that session runs inside tmux, because tmux is how the daemon delivers keystrokes and captures the screen. There are two ways to get a controllable session:

  • Start it from the terminal with porthole wrap:

    cd ~/code/my-project
porthole wrap claude            # or: porthole wrap codex
porthole wrap claude --resume   # extra arguments go to the CLI

    wrap opens a tmux session in the current directory and runs the CLI in it, attaching your terminal as usual. Inside tmux already? It opens a new window instead of nesting.

  • Start it from the app with New session. Those always run inside tmux (named ph-<provider>-<id>), and you can attach to them from a terminal too.

A session started any other way (plain claude in a terminal, an IDE integration) is shown read-only: you can follow it, but the input bar and the terminal view are disabled. Once it has finished, Resume in tmux… restarts it under tmux and makes it controllable.

docs.title: Choosing where sessions start
docs.text:
New session lists the repositories the daemon offers. porthole repos prints the same list, which comes from three sources:

  1. Recent: every directory the daemon has seen a Claude Code or Codex session in, from the profiles it watches. Nothing to configure; if you have used an agent in a repository, it is here.

  2. Repositories recorded with porthole add (or listed under repos in config.toml). Use this for a repository you have not run an agent in yet:

    cd ~/code/new-project
porthole add            # finds the git top level, asks to confirm
porthole add ~/code/other-project --yes

  3. Workspaces: parent folders scanned two levels deep for git repositories, recorded with porthole add --workspace ~/code (or listed under workspaces in config.toml).

porthole add writes to ~/.config/porthole/repos.toml, a file the CLI manages; your hand-written config.toml is never rewritten. A running daemon picks the change up immediately; otherwise it applies at the next start. porthole remove [dir] takes an entry out again (entries you wrote in config.toml yourself are edited there). The daemon logs a warning at start when no repositories or workspaces are configured, but recent directories still work.

For safety, a new session's directory must be inside a configured repository or workspace, or be one of the recent directories; the app cannot start an agent in an arbitrary path.

docs.title: Hooks: permission prompts and status
docs.text:
porthole install (or porthole install-hooks) registers Porthole as a Claude Code hook for SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, Notification, PermissionRequest and PostModelSwitch, and as the Codex notify handler. That is how the daemon learns a session's status (idle, busy, waiting for permission, waiting for input, exited) without polling, and how a permission prompt reaches the phone.

When Claude Code asks for permission:

  1. The hook sends the request to the daemon and waits.
  2. The daemon shows it to every connected phone (and sends a push if a relay is configured) with the tool name and input.
  3. Tap Allow or Deny. The answer goes back through the hook, bound to that request's id, so a stale approval can never apply to a different prompt.
  4. If nobody answers within permission_timeout_s (60 s by default), the hook steps aside and Claude Code shows its own prompt in the terminal, exactly as if Porthole were not there. The same happens if the daemon is not running.

Hooks take effect for sessions started after they were installed; running sessions keep their old hook set. porthole uninstall-hooks removes them (Codex's notify line is removed by hand).

docs.title: Status and attention
docs.text: Each session carries a status: idle, busy, waiting_permission, waiting_input, exited or unknown. Sessions that need you sort to the top of the home screen. With Notify while connected on, the app raises a local notification for permission prompts and input requests while it is open, and on Android also in the background when Stay connected in the background is on. For notifications while the app is closed, see Push notifications.

docs.title: Multiple machines
docs.text: Pair the phone with each machine (laptop, workstation, a box in the rack). Each runs its own daemon with its own pairing; the app merges their sessions into one list and lets you filter by machine.

docs.title: Accounts and usage
docs.text: If claude-swap is on the machine's PATH, the daemon reads its cached account list and the app shows the active account and quota windows under Accounts & usage, and tags each session with the account doing the work. Turn it off with [cswap] enabled = false in config.toml.

docs.title: iOS background behavior
docs.text:
iOS suspends an app's network connections shortly after it leaves the foreground. Porthole keeps the WebSocket open while the app is visible and for the short grace period iOS allows afterwards; after that no notifications can arrive from the daemon directly.

What that means in practice:

  • With the app open, permission prompts and "needs input" states appear live.
  • With the phone locked or the app in the background, nothing arrives until you open the app again. Porthole reconnects automatically and shows the current state immediately.
  • Android can keep the connection alive with a foreground service (a persistent notification), so Android users get timely alerts without any cloud service.

The only way to wake an iOS app from the outside is Apple's push service, which requires a server holding the app's push key. That is what the optional push relay is for: the daemon sends an encrypted wake-up through a small relay you run or are given a URL for (see Push notifications), the phone wakes, brings the VPN up on demand, and fetches the details from your machine. Nothing about your sessions leaves the VPN; the relay sees a device token and ciphertext.

docs.title: Store privacy answers
docs.text: Maintainer answer sheet for App Store Connect (App Privacy) and Google Play Console (Data safety), kept in step with https://zerkersec.io/privacy. Update both forms whenever section 6 or 7 of the policy changes. Last reviewed 2026-11-12.

docs.title: Shared facts
docs.text:
• Privacy policy URL: https://zerkersec.io/privacy. Terms: https://zerkersec.io/terms.
  • In-app link: Settings → "Privacy policy" and "Terms of service" (app/lib/screens/settings.dart).
  • No accounts in the app. No in-app purchases. No ads. No analytics or crash-reporting SDK. The app has a built-in demo machine ("Try the demo" on the first screen) that reviewers can use.
  • Third-party SDKs that touch the network: Firebase Core + Firebase Messaging (push token only; analytics deactivated in AndroidManifest.xml and Info.plist). mobile_scanner scans QR codes on device; on Android it uses Google ML Kit's barcode model, which processes frames locally.
  • Permissions: INTERNET, CAMERA (QR pairing), POST_NOTIFICATIONS, FOREGROUND_SERVICE and FOREGROUND_SERVICE_DATA_SYNC (keeps the VPN socket alive while a session is open). iOS: NSCameraUsageDescription.
  • Data the app sends to the developer's servers: only when the user pastes a relay URL for the developer-hosted relay and turns push on. Then the relay receives the credential from that URL, a random device id, platform and the push token, and the daemon later sends encrypted notices the relay cannot read. The relay operator (the developer, for the hosted relay) links the device id to the website account the credential belongs to. Users who paste their own relay's URL send nothing to the developer. Everything else stays between the phone and the user's own computer over their VPN.
  • The developer account is an individual. Apple shows the legal name as the seller; Google shows the legal name, country and developer email. No address is shown because the app is free with no in-app purchases, so there is no "monetised" trigger.

docs.title: Apple: App Privacy (App Store Connect)
docs.text:
Question Answer Do you or your third-party partners collect data from this app? Yes Contact Info Not collected (the supporter email is handled on the website, not in the app) Identifiers → Device ID Collected. Linked to the user: Yes (the hosted relay records the device id against the website account whose credential was used). Used for tracking: No. Purpose: App Functionality. (The random push device id and the push token, sent to the relay only when push is on.) User Content, Usage Data, Diagnostics, Location, Financial, Health, Browsing, Search, Purchases, Contacts, Sensitive Info Not collected Tracking No. NSPrivacyTracking is false in app/ios/Runner/PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy. Privacy manifest app/ios/Runner/PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy: DeviceID collected, linked, App Functionality; UserDefaults accessed for reason CA92.1.

Note: the camera is used for QR scanning only; images are not collected, so no Photos or Videos data type applies.

docs.title: Google: Data safety (Play Console)
docs.text:
Section Answer Does your app collect or share any of the required user data types? Yes Is all user data encrypted in transit? Yes (TLS to the daemon with certificate pinning; HTTPS to the relay) Do you provide a way for users to request data deletion? Yes: remove the relay in Settings, unpair the phone on the daemon, delete the account at zerkersec.io/supporter (hosted relay users), or email privacy@zerkersec.io Device or other IDs Collected: yes. Shared: yes, with Google (FCM push token) as a service provider. Ephemeral: no. Required: optional (only when push is enabled). Purpose: App functionality. App activity, App info and performance (crash logs, diagnostics), Personal info, Financial, Location, Messages, Photos and videos, Audio, Files, Calendar, Contacts, Health Not collected Does the app use any security practices? Data encrypted in transit; users can request deletion; follows the Families policy: not applicable (not directed at children) Independent security review No

Camera: used for QR codes only, frames are processed on device and discarded; nothing to declare under Photos and videos.

docs.title: Other console answers
docs.text:
• Encryption / export compliance (Apple): the app uses only standard, published algorithms (TLS, X25519, HKDF-SHA256, XChaCha20-Poly1305) for its own protocol, so ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption is false in Info.plist. Aaron confirms the exemption reading and files the annual self-classification report with BIS if it applies to him.
  • Foreground service (Play, dataSync): "Keeps the connection to the user's own computer open while they watch a session, so prompts arrive without a cloud service. Started only from the Settings switch, stopped from the same switch or by closing the app." Attach the demo recording.
  • IP addresses: Cloudflare's short-lived request logs apply to the relay (policy section 3); not a collected data type in either form.

docs.title: Keep these in sync
docs.text:
• zerkersec.io/privacy sections 6 and 7 (what the app and relay keep).
  • app/ios/Runner/PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy (collected data types and required-reason APIs).
  • app/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml (analytics flags, permissions).
  • This file, and the two store forms.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Porthole's threat model, produced with the rafter-secure-design auth and threat-modeling walks before any auth or control-plane code was written. It is updated when a boundary changes. For the practical side (pairing, revoking a phone, what a relay sees) see Pair a phone and Push notifications.

docs.title: Data-flow diagram
docs.text:
[Phone app] ──wss (VPN only, pinned cert, bearer device token)──┐
                                                                 ▼
                                                     [porthole daemon, runs as the user]
                                                       │   │        │          │
            transcript JSONL (read) ◄──────────────────┘   │        │          └──► [tmux] send-keys / capture-pane / pipe-pane
            ~/.claude/projects, ~/.codex/sessions          │        │
                                                           │        └──► [cswap list --json] (read, optional)
   [claude / codex hook process] ──unix socket 0600──────►─┘
                                                           │
   [Cloudflare Worker relay] ◄──https {grant, ciphertext}──┘ (opt-in, Supporter only)
          │
          └──► [FCM] ──► [Apple/Google push] ──► [Phone]

Trust boundaries:

  1. Phone ↔ daemon (VPN network). Control point: TLS pinning + device token.
  2. Hook process ↔ daemon (local unix socket). Control point: filesystem permission.
  3. Daemon ↔ tmux and transcript files (same user). No boundary; the daemon is as privileged as the user. This is the blast radius if the daemon is compromised.
  4. Daemon ↔ relay ↔ FCM (internet). Control point: signed grant, encrypted payload.
  5. Store app ↔ relay (internet). Control point: supporter key checked against the entitlement service, plus Play Integrity attestation when ATTEST_MODE is on (off by default; App Attest not implemented).

docs.title: Auth decisions (docs/auth.md walk)
docs.text:
• Identity. End users are the device owner's phones; there are no accounts. Identity is the paired device. Hooks are local processes of the same OS user. The relay authenticates the app by the credential in its relay URL (and, when ATTEST_MODE is on, by platform attestation) and the daemon only indirectly, via a grant the app obtained.
  • AuthN primitive. Opaque random 32-byte device tokens, stored on the daemon as SHA-256 hashes in devices.json (0600), presented as Authorization: Bearer over TLS. Not JWT: there is one verifier, revocation must be instant, and nothing needs to be self-contained. Pairing codes are 8 random base32 chars, single use, 120 s TTL, compared in constant time, max 5 attempts per minute per source address.
  • TLS. Daemon generates an ECDSA P-256 self-signed certificate on first run (valid 10 years, SAN = the configured bind addresses). The QR carries its SHA-256 SPKI fingerprint; the app pins that fingerprint and refuses anything else. No CA, no system trust store. TLS 1.3 only.
  • AuthZ model. Flat: any paired device may do anything the daemon can do. This is explicit. Per-device scopes (read-only devices, per-workspace devices) are a v2 item with a scopes field already reserved in devices.json so it needs no migration.
  • Token lifetime and revocation. Device tokens do not expire; they are revoked by porthole devices revoke <id> or by deleting the entry, and the WebSocket for that device is closed within one second. Pairing codes are removed on use or expiry. Push grants expire at min(subscription renewal, 30 days) and are revocable by device id at the relay.
  • Service-to-service. Daemon → relay carries the device's grant, not a daemon identity; the relay never trusts a daemon per se. Hook → daemon is trusted by socket ownership (0600, in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR or ~/.porthole).
  • Refuse-list check. No passwords, no homegrown JWT (grants are PASETO v4.public via a maintained library, or Ed25519-signed JSON with a pinned algorithm), no trusted-network assumptions beyond the unix socket, no tenant ids from requests.

docs.title: 1. Phone ↔ daemon
docs.text:
• S Token theft from a lost phone: tokens live in Keychain/Keystore, optional biometric lock in app, instant revocation on the daemon. Token theft on the wire: TLS 1.3 with pinning; a rogue AP on the VPN path sees ciphertext only. Spoofed daemon: pinning fails closed.
  • T All traffic is TLS; messages are JSON validated against proto/ schemas with size caps (64 KiB per message, 1 MiB per history page).
  • R The daemon logs structured warnings (device id, error) through slog; there is no per-action audit log. Accepted for a single-user tool; a device's last_seen in devices.json is the only persistent trace of use.
  • I Error responses are generic (unauthorized, bad_request). No transcript content in logs. /v1/health returns only ok and version to authenticated callers; unauthenticated callers get 401 with no body. Session titles and cwd paths are sent to paired devices only.
  • D Per-connection message rate limit (60 msg/s, burst 120), max 4 concurrent connections per device, pairing endpoint rate limit, pane.bytes back-pressure (drop and resend snapshot) so a chatty TUI cannot queue unbounded memory.
  • E None available: all devices are equal and equal to the user. Mitigation for the blast radius is the bind policy (nothing reachable off the VPN) and revocation.

docs.title: 2. Hook ↔ daemon
docs.text:
• S Any process running as the user can connect to the socket and claim to be a hook. That process could already do anything the user can, so this is not an escalation. The daemon still validates the hook payload shape and only acts on events whose transcript_path resolves inside a watched profile.
  • T/I Socket is 0600 in a 0700 directory. Permission decisions are sent back on the same connection only.
  • D A hook that waits for a phone answer blocks the CLI. Timeout is configurable (default 60 s) and the hook exits with no decision on timeout, socket error, or daemon absence, so Claude Code falls back to its own prompt.

docs.title: 3. Daemon ↔ tmux and files
docs.text:
• The daemon runs as the user, never root, and refuses to start as uid 0. send-keys is passed with -l (literal) and the text as a separate argv element, never through a shell. Session and pane targets are validated against the set the daemon discovered, not taken from the client as free text. Spawn commands use a fixed argv (claude, codex plus allowlisted flags) with the working directory validated after symlink resolution: it must be inside a configured workspace or added repository, or be exactly a directory an agent session has already run in on this machine.
  • Transcript reads are read-only. Offsets are tracked per real path so a symlinked profile is not read twice.

docs.title: 4 and 5. Relay
docs.text:
• S A grant is minted only for an active supporter key (the relay asks the entitlement service) and, when ATTEST_MODE is on, only for a store build attested by Play Integrity. The grant binds the device id and push token.
  • T Grants are signed (Ed25519) by a key that exists only as a Worker secret. Push payloads are encrypted (XChaCha20-Poly1305) with a key agreed at pairing, so the relay, FCM, and the platforms see ciphertext.
  • I The relay learns the relay credential, device id, platform and push token at grant time, the IP addresses of phone and daemon, and per push the fact that "device X was pushed at time T" plus an opaque SHA-256 digest of the session key used as the collapse id. It never sees the notice content. The privacy policy at zerkersec.io/privacy states this.
  • D Rate-limit bindings per device id (10/min) and per IP on grant (5/min), a 300/day KV counter per device, payload cap 480 bytes, free-plan hard cap of 100k requests/day fails closed on push only. KV deny list for revoked device ids.
  • E A stolen grant can push only to its own device.

docs.title: Negative space
docs.text:
• Assumed safe: the VPN itself, the user's own machine, and the two CLIs' transcript formats. The first two are out of scope by design. The third is mitigated by parsers that ignore unknown entries and fixture tests pinned to observed formats.
  • Worst single compromise: the daemon process. It has the user's full access anyway, so the control that matters is not letting anyone reach it: bind policy refuses public addresses, and a public bind requires an explicit flag with an alarming name.
  • Attacker goals: read private code and conversations (needs VPN access plus a device token), drive the agent to exfiltrate or destroy (same), spam pushes (needs a valid relay credential and, when attestation is on, a genuine store build), run up Aaron's bill (hard cap, no bill).
  • Incident controls: porthole devices revoke per device, relay deny list per device id, relay grant key rotation via a new Worker secret (existing grants stop verifying at once; apps re-mint within three days).

docs.title: Abuse twins
docs.text:
• Pair a phone → attacker on the VPN brute-forces pairing codes: 8 base32 chars, 120 s TTL, 5 attempts/min, single use.
  • Send input to a session → attacker injects commands into tmux: requires a device token; input is literal, never shell-interpreted.
  • Approve a permission from the phone → stale approval applied to a different prompt: approvals carry the hook's request id and expire with it.
  • Spawn a session in a repo → path traversal outside workspaces: resolved path must be inside a configured workspace or added repository, or equal a directory of a known session. A paired phone can therefore start an agent only where you already run one or where you ran porthole add.
  • Subscribe to pane bytes → memory exhaustion from a fast TUI: bounded ring buffer per subscriber with snapshot resync.

docs.title: Residual risks accepted
docs.text:
• A paired device is fully trusted. Single-user tool; per-device scopes are v2.
  • Hook socket trusts any same-user process. Equivalent to the user's own shell access.
  • Audit log is not tamper-evident. Single-user tool.
  • iOS background delivery depends on Apple's push service and a relay; users without a relay have foreground-only notifications on iOS. Documented.

docs.title: Follow-ups
docs.text:
• Tests: bind policy refusal, pairing brute-force limit, token revocation closes sockets, send-keys argv never passes through a shell, workspace path containment, pane buffer bound.
  • rafter-code-review plus rafter run on internal/server, internal/tmux, internal/hooks, and relay/ before each release.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Start with porthole doctor on the machine and porthole status; most problems show up there. Daemon logs: journalctl --user -u porthole -f on Linux, /tmp/porthole.log for the launchd agent on macOS, or run porthole serve --log-level debug in a terminal.

docs.title: Pairing and connecting
docs.text: porthole pair says "no VPN or private address is bound" The daemon found nothing but loopback to listen on. Bring the VPN up (or join the Wi-Fi) and restart the daemon; listen = ["auto"] picks up private and VPN addresses at start. The app cannot reach the machine The phone needs a private route to the host shown by porthole pair: the same network, or the VPN connected on the phone too. Public addresses are refused by design. Check that TCP port 7433 (or your port) is open in the host firewall on that interface, and that porthole status lists the address you are using. "Certificate fingerprint mismatch" The daemon's certificate changed, usually because its state directory (~/.local/state/porthole/) was deleted or the daemon moved to a new machine. Forget the machine in the app and pair again. The pairing code is rejected Codes are single use and expire after two minutes. Five wrong attempts in a minute lock that source address out for a minute. Run porthole pair again. A phone was lost porthole devices then porthole devices revoke <id>. Its connections close within a second and its token stops working.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text: A session is read-only Only sessions running inside tmux can be controlled. Start them with porthole wrap claude (or codex), or from the app's New session. A finished session can be restarted under tmux with Resume in tmux…. See Sessions. A session is missing The daemon reads ~/.claude/projects and ~/.codex/sessions. A CLI using another CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR or CODEX_HOME is found while it runs; add the directory to profiles in config.toml to watch it always. Check porthole sessions. No repositories in New session Nothing has been recorded and no session has run anywhere yet. Run porthole add inside a repository, or porthole add --workspace ~/code for a folder of them, then check porthole repos. Permission prompts do not appear on the phone Hooks apply only to sessions started after porthole install-hooks ran; restart the session. porthole doctor reports whether each profile has the hooks. Prompts also fall back to the terminal after permission_timeout_s (60 s) with no answer, so an old prompt may already have been answered at the keyboard. Session status stays "unknown" Same cause: the status comes from hooks, so sessions started before the hooks were installed report nothing until restarted. No account or quota information claude-swap must be on the daemon's PATH. The systemd unit and launchd agent set a fixed PATH; edit it if cswap lives elsewhere, and [cswap] enabled must not be false.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: Nothing arrives while the app is closed Direct notifications need the app open (or, on Android, Stay connected in the background). Everything else needs a push relay: a relay URL in Settings → Push relay, [push] relay_url set on every machine, and the daemon restarted afterwards. See Push notifications. "Relay: not active" The relay answered 402: the credential in your relay URL is not active (lapsed, unknown, or mistyped). Check it with whoever runs the relay; for the hosted relay that is https://zerkersec.io/supporter. "Relay: could not verify" The relay could not be reached. The app keeps using its last grant and retries; Re-check forces a retry now. "Apple has not issued this phone a push token yet" The app asks Apple for a push token the first time you save a relay URL, and Apple can take a few seconds. Make sure the phone is online, then save the URL again. Builds older than 2026-11-22 never asked Apple at all and fail here every time; update the app. Relay is connected but one machine never pushes That daemon has no relay_url, or the machine is muted under Machines. The daemon refuses push registrations until the URL is set and it is restarted. There is no Push relay field in Settings This build was made without the Firebase options, so it cannot receive push at all. Install a store build, or build with --dart-define-from-file=dart_defines/store.json. iOS alerts arrive late or not at all without a relay Expected: iOS suspends the connection shortly after the app leaves the foreground. See iOS background behavior.

docs.title: The daemon
docs.text: "refusing to run as root" Run the daemon as the user who owns the sessions. The service files do this already; do not wrap them in sudo. "listen ... is a public address; refusing" An explicit listen entry is a public IP. Use a private or VPN address instead. --allow-public-bind-i-understand exists but is not the intended deployment. The service does not come back after a reboot (Linux) User services only run while you are logged in unless linger is enabled: sudo loginctl enable-linger "$USER". porthole install tries this and prints the command if it could not. claude or codex not found by the daemon but fine in a shell The service runs with a fixed PATH (~/.local/bin, /usr/local/bin, /usr/bin, /bin, plus /opt/homebrew/bin on macOS). Add the directory your CLI lives in to the unit's Environment=PATH=… line (Linux) or the plist's PATH (macOS), or point binary in config.toml at the full path. Changes to config.toml do nothing Only repos.toml and workspaces reload live (on SIGHUP or when porthole add runs). Everything else needs systemctl --user restart porthole. See Reloading.

docs.title: Self-hosting the push relay
docs.text: The relay is only needed for background push on phones. Everything else in Porthole works without it. The app takes any relay URL in Settings → Push relay; the project hosts one for its supporters (https://zerkersec.io/supporter hands out a personal URL; see Push notifications), and this page is how to run your own.

docs.title: The relay URL
docs.text: The app accepts https://[credential@]host[/path]. The optional userinfo is the relay credential: the app sends it as Authorization: Bearer on the grant request and never interprets it. A relay with ENTITLEMENT_STATIC_KEYS hands out credentials of the form PH-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX; a relay backed by an entitlement service uses whatever that service issues. The daemon only needs the base URL (no credential) in [push] relay_url.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
Secret / var Purpose GRANT_SIGNING_KEY Ed25519 private key (PKCS8, base64url) that signs push grants. Generate: node -e "crypto.subtle.generateKey({name:'Ed25519'},true,['sign','verify']).then(async k=>console.log(Buffer.from(await crypto.subtle.exportKey('pkcs8',k.privateKey)).toString('base64url')))" FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT Firebase service account JSON with the Firebase Cloud Messaging API role FCM_PROJECT_ID (var) Firebase project id (optional; read from the service account otherwise) ENTITLEMENT_URL (var) + ENTITLEMENT_SECRET an HTTPS endpoint that answers whether a credential is active (see below) ENTITLEMENT_STATIC_KEYS (var) alternative for a personal relay: comma-separated SHA-256 hex hashes of the credentials you hand out yourself ATTEST_MODE (var) off, android (Play Integrity) or all; iOS App Attest is not yet implemented, so all refuses iOS grants. The store builds send no attestation today, so leave it off for them DENY (KV) revoked device ids and daily counters

Keep the origin of record for every secret outside the repo; set them with wrangler secret put.

docs.title: The entitlement contract
docs.text: The relay never decides who may push. It calls POST $ENTITLEMENT_URL with Authorization: Bearer $ENTITLEMENT_SECRET and body {"key": "<credential>", "device_id": "...", "platform": "ios|android"} and expects {"active": true|false, "period_end": "<ISO 8601>", "level": 0, "tier": null, "reason": "..."}. level and tier are optional: a tier level (1 and up) and its name, passed back to the app on the grant response. Omit them or send 0 for a flat yes/no. Status 404 means unknown credential, 429 means too many devices on that credential. The grant it mints expires at period_end or 30 days, whichever is sooner, and the app re-mints within three days of expiry, so revoking a credential on your side takes effect by the next refresh. Any backend that follows this contract works; Porthole's own is the supporter service at zerkersec.io.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
cd relay
npm install
npx wrangler kv namespace create DENY     # put the id into wrangler.jsonc
# remove the "routes" entry in wrangler.jsonc (it is the project's custom domain)
npx wrangler secret put GRANT_SIGNING_KEY
npx wrangler secret put FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT
npx wrangler secret put ENTITLEMENT_SECRET   # or set ENTITLEMENT_STATIC_KEYS as a var
npx wrangler deploy

The store builds already carry the Firebase options; paste https://<credential>@your-worker.workers.dev into Settings → Push relay. A self-built app needs the Firebase options compiled in (--dart-define-from-file=dart_defines/store.json with your own project's FB_API_KEY, FB_APP_ID, FB_SENDER_ID, FB_PROJECT_ID and, on iOS, FB_IOS_BUNDLE_ID). Set relay_url in the daemon config to the base URL.

docs.title: How a push travels
docs.text:
1. The user pastes a relay URL into the app, which obtains a platform push token from FCM.
  2. The app asks the relay for a grant: POST /v1/grant with the credential as a bearer token. The relay asks the entitlement service whether it is active and returns a signed grant binding the device id and push token, valid for at most 30 days.
  3. The app hands the grant to each paired daemon over the VPN.
  4. When a session needs you and the phone is not connected, the daemon encrypts a tiny notice with the key agreed at pairing and posts {grant, ct} to the relay.
  5. The relay checks the signature, expiry, deny list and rate limits, then sends the ciphertext through FCM. The phone decrypts it and shows the notification, and the app fetches details from the daemon on open.

The relay never sees session content, repository names or prompts. It sees a push token, a device id and a timestamp.

docs.title: Blocking a device
docs.text: npx wrangler kv key put --binding DENY <device-id> 1

docs.title: Rotating the grant key
docs.text: Set a new GRANT_SIGNING_KEY; existing grants stop verifying immediately and apps re-mint on their next refresh (within three days of a grant's expiry).
